kurals.tamil:
தாம்வீழ்வார் தம்வீழப் பெற்றவர் பெற்றாரே
காமத்துக் காழில் கனி.
kurals.transliteration:
Thaamveezhvaar thamveezhap petravar petraare
kaamaththuk kaazhil kani.
kurals.meaning: Those who are loved in return by the very one they love have won love’s best prize: a fruit with no hard stone inside, all sweetness.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you save half your sandwich for your best friend, and your best friend has saved half of theirs for you. That happy feeling of sharing both ways is like biting into a fruit with no pit at all: nothing hard to spoil it.
kurals.university: Chapter 120, tanippaṭar mikuti (‘the excess of solitary suffering’), belongs to the karpiyal (married love) sequence on separation; in the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar the heroine, left alone, fears that her longing is not matched by her absent husband’s and speaks to her confidante (tōḻi). The chapter opens by defining what she lacks: tām vīḻvār tam vīḻap peṟṟavar, those whom the ones they desire (vīḻ, ‘to desire, fall for’) desire in turn. Kāḻ il kaṉi is ‘a fruit without a stone (kāḻ)’, i.e. pleasure without any hard residue of pain; Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both gloss it as the seedless fruit that is the yield (payaṉ) of married love. Pope renders: ‘The bliss to be beloved by those they love who gains, / Of love the stoneless, luscious fruit obtains.’ The couplet is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In that family, where the husband is pleased with his wife and the wife with her husband, happiness will assuredly be lasting.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu’s household code makes lasting happiness depend on the delight being mutual, the husband pleased with the wife and the wife with the husband.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘stoneless fruit’ is exactly this two-way pleasure, which Manu calls the secure root of a happy home.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a close match on mutual delight in marriage, though Manu speaks of domestic stability rather than the Kural’s image of love’s fruit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My beloved is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies.”
christianity.explanation: The bride in the Song of Solomon sums up her joy in a single line of perfect reciprocity.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Mine, and I am his’ is the Kural’s condition for the seedless fruit: the one I love loves me.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; near one-to-one on mutual belonging, though without the fruit metaphor.

islam.quote_or_event: “There is nothing like marriage, for two who love one another.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says that for two people who already love each other, nothing compares with marriage.
islam.tie_back: Both texts single out love that runs both ways as the best thing married life can give.
islam.source: Sunan Ibn Majah 1847 (graded hasan by Darussalam)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; strong match on mutual love fulfilled in marriage.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine, That feedeth among the lilies.”
judaism.explanation: The Shulammite states the reciprocity of love as a balanced formula, her belonging to him matched by his to her.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s happy lovers are those for whom this formula is true in both directions.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); near one-to-one on reciprocal love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The householders Nakula’s father and Nakula’s mother tell the Buddha that since their youthful marriage neither has been unfaithful even in thought, and that they wish to see each other in this life and the next; the Buddha teaches that a couple matched in faith, virtue, generosity and discernment will meet again.
buddhism.explanation: The Samajivina discourse treats a wholly mutual marriage as a real good worth wishing to prolong.
buddhism.tie_back: Nakula’s parents are the Buddhist picture of the Kural’s fortunate pair whose love is returned in full.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested sutta; strong fit on mutual marital love, though the Buddhist frame is shared virtue rather than sweetness of desire.

jainism.quote_or_event: Among the lay vows, the vow of chastity for a householder is framed as svadāra-santoṣa, contentment with one’s own spouse, which channels desire into a single faithful marriage.
jainism.explanation: Jain householder ethics do not praise love’s sweetness, but they do honour a marriage in which each partner’s desire rests contentedly on the other alone.
jainism.tie_back: The closest Jain counterpart to the Kural’s fortunate lovers is the householder couple content in each other, though Jainism ranks even this below renunciation.
jainism.source: Ratnakaranda Shravakachara, on the vow of brahmacarya-anuvrata (paraphrase; cf. tr. Champat Rai Jain)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a standard Jain teaching on lay chastity; only a next-best match, since Jain texts treat marital love as a limit on desire, not as a fruit to be savoured.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus wishes the young princess Nausicaa a husband and a home of one mind, saying there is nothing better or nobler than when husband and wife keep house together in harmony, a grief to their enemies and a joy to their friends.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer has his hero name like-mindedness between husband and wife as the greatest blessing of life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s seedless fruit and Homer’s best of all gifts are the same thing: two hearts that agree.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 6.180-185 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; strong fit on reciprocal harmony as life’s highest good.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that the friendship of husband and wife is natural and can include usefulness, pleasure and, where both are good, virtue, each delighting in the other’s goodness.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the best marriage is a friendship in which the good and the pleasure flow both ways.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s happiest lovers are Aristotle’s married friends, whose delight is returned in kind.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good thematic fit on reciprocal conjugal friendship, though Aristotle’s register is analytic rather than lyrical.

kurals.tamil:
வாழ்வார்க்கு வானம் பயந்தற்றால் வீழ்வார்க்கு
வீழ்வார் அளிக்கும் அளி.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaazhvaarkku vaanam payandhatraal veezhvaarkku
veezhvaar alikkum ali.
kurals.meaning: The tenderness a lover shows to the one who loves him is like rain from the sky to those whose life depends on it.
kurals.elementary: Think of a thirsty garden in summer. When the rain finally comes, every leaf perks up. When someone you love is kind to you, your heart perks up the same way.
kurals.university: The couplet sets the beloved’s aḷi (grace, tender kindness) beside the rain that the sky (vāṉam) yields (payanta) to living beings (vāḻvār), echoing the Kural’s own chapter on rain (vāṉ ciṟappu, ch. 2). Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators take vāḻvār as ‘those who live by it’ and insist on timeliness: Pappaiah stresses rain at the proper season, and Kalaignar reads it as lovers meeting at the right time. The point in this chapter is implicit contrast: the heroine is the parched field to whom no such rain is coming. Pope: ‘As heaven on living men showers blessings from above, / Is tender grace by lovers shown to those they love.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna teaches that living beings are sustained by food, food is produced from rain, and rain comes from sacrifice, so that the whole order of life hangs on the rain that falls in due season.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita presents rain as the link on which all living beings depend.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural borrows exactly this dependence of life on rain to describe how a loving spouse’s kindness keeps the beloved alive.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.14 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; matches only the rain-sustains-life simile, not its application to love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “he shall come unto us as the rain, as the latter and former rain unto the earth.”
christianity.explanation: Hosea pictures the coming of the beloved Lord to his people as seasonal rain on dry ground.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hosea likens the arrival of love to rain that revives those who wait for it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV (excerpt); the rain-as-love image matches well, though Hosea’s love is divine, not marital.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an names as one of God’s signs that He created spouses for people so that they may find tranquillity in them, placing affection and mercy between them; a few verses later it names as another sign the rain He sends down to give life to the earth after its death.
islam.explanation: Surah ar-Rum sets marital affection and life-giving rain side by side among the signs of divine care.
islam.tie_back: The Kural joins the same two signs into one simile: a spouse’s kindness is rain to the one who lives by it.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of two nearby verses; the pairing is suggestive but the Qur’an does not itself make the comparison.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that any man who has no wife lives without joy, without blessing and without goodness.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis treat the love of a spouse as the source from which joy and blessing reach a person’s life.
judaism.tie_back: As the Kural says love is rain to the one who lives by it, the Talmud says a life without that love is dry of joy and blessing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known dictum; it matches love as life-giving, but lacks the rain image and is framed from the husband’s side.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Dhaniya Sutta a contented cowherd, his roof thatched and his fire lit, tells the sky it may rain if it likes, praising his wife as faithful, long his companion and pleasing to him; the Buddha answers each verse with his own freedom from all such supports.
buddhism.explanation: The herdsman’s security rests on a loving wife and on rain that can do him no harm, while the Buddha points beyond both.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s rain-and-love pairing appears here too, though the Buddhist sutta finally sets both aside in favour of non-attachment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the rain-and-wife pairing is genuine, but the sutta’s point runs against the Kural’s dependence on love.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Tamil Jain epic Jivaka Chintamani, the hero Jivaka wins and marries a series of brides, and the poet dwells on the mutual delight of each newly united couple before Jivaka finally renounces the world.
jainism.explanation: The Jain epic describes reciprocal married love with real warmth, while framing it as a stage to be outgrown.
jainism.tie_back: Its scenes of shared delight answer the Kural’s picture of a lover’s kindness falling like rain, though the Jain poem ends in renunciation.
jainism.source: Tiruttakkatevar, Jivaka Chintamani (paraphrase of the epic’s marriage episodes)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from a Tamil Jain text, used as a next-best match; it lacks the rain image and its arc favours renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In a fragment of Aeschylus’ lost Danaids, Aphrodite says the holy sky longs to wed the earth and the earth longs for union; rain falls from the bridegroom sky and the earth conceives pasture for flocks and grain for mortals.
greek_mythology.explanation: Aphrodite herself presents rain as the act of love by which heaven gives life to the earth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s simile run in reverse: rain is love, as for the Kural love is rain.
greek_mythology.source: Aeschylus, Danaids, fragment 44 (Radt), preserved in Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 13.600b (paraphrase)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested fragment; a strong image match on love as life-giving rain.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Boethius’ Lady Philosophy sings that it is love which holds earth and sea together and rules the heavens, keeping the seasons in their order; if love slackened its reins, everything now bound in concord would fall into war.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius makes love the force that keeps the whole cosmos, seasons included, alive and in order.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s comparison of love to life-sustaining rain fits Boethius’ claim that love is what keeps the world going.
philosophy.source: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2, metre 8 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a cosmic rather than personal love, so only a partial fit.

kurals.tamil:
வீழுநர் வீழப் படுவார்க்கு அமையுமே
வாழுநம் என்னும் செருக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Veezhunar veezhap paduvaarkku amaiyume
vaazhunam ennum serukku.
kurals.meaning: Only a woman truly loved by the one she loves can carry the proud confidence that says, ‘We shall live happily yet,’ even while he is away.
kurals.elementary: If your mom goes on a trip and you know she loves you and will come back, you can wait bravely and even smile. Knowing you are loved makes waiting easier.
kurals.university: Vīḻunar vīḻappaṭuvār is ‘those who are desired by the ones who desire them’; for such women alone amaiyumē (it is fitting) to hold the ceruukku (pride, proud confidence) of saying vāḻunam, ‘we shall live (in joy).’ In the separation context Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar read the pride as forward-looking: despite present parting, the loved wife can be sure that reunion and happiness will come; Pappaiah adds ‘by the certainty that he will soon return.’ The heroine’s unspoken complaint is that she cannot claim this pride. Pope: ‘Who love and are beloved to them alone / Belongs the boast, “We’ve made life’s very joys our own.”’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Yama comes for her husband Satyavan, the devoted Savitri follows the god of death, and her steadfast love and wisdom win back Satyavan’s life so that the two can return home together.
hinduism.explanation: Savitri’s certainty in a love that is mutual gives her the courage to argue with Death himself.
hinduism.tie_back: Savitri embodies the Kural’s ‘we shall live’ confidence that belongs to the wife who knows her love is shared.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva (Savitri episode) (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; it shows confidence born of mutual love, though Savitri’s trial is death rather than ordinary separation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Solomon declares love able to survive every flood that might overwhelm it.
christianity.tie_back: This is the ground of the loved wife’s confidence in the Kural: real, returned love will outlast the present separation.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV (excerpt); love’s endurance fits, though the verse does not single out love that is returned.

islam.quote_or_event: In the hadith of Umm Zar‘, Aisha relates eleven women describing their husbands; Umm Zar‘ proudly recalls a husband who treated her with lavish kindness, and the Prophet tells Aisha that he is to her as Abu Zar‘ was to Umm Zar‘.
islam.explanation: A wife’s happy boast about a loving husband is affirmed by the Prophet as true of his own marriage.
islam.tie_back: Umm Zar‘’s pride is the ‘boast’ the Kural says belongs only to a wife whose love is returned.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Marriage, hadith of Umm Zar‘ (paraphrase)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith, cited without a number because it was not checked live; good fit on a loved wife’s proud confidence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “for love is strong as death, jealousy is cruel as the grave; the flashes thereof are flashes of fire, a very flame of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Song’s climax claims for love a strength equal to death itself.
judaism.tie_back: The loved wife of the Kural can say ‘we shall live’ because she trusts a love as strong as this.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917, excerpt); love’s strength fits, but the verse is not about separation or mutuality as such.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Describing seven kinds of wives, the Buddha praises the wife who is like a friend: she rejoices on seeing her husband as one rejoices at seeing a long-absent companion.
buddhism.explanation: The ‘friend-wife’ of this sutta is marked by glad, confident affection toward her husband.
buddhism.tie_back: Her joy at reunion is the Kural’s ‘we shall live’, available only where affection runs both ways.
buddhism.source: Bhariya Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya, Book of Sevens (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; cited without a sutta number because Anguttara numbering varies by edition; partial fit, as the sutta catalogues wives’ conduct rather than mutual love.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain story of Shripal and Mayanasundari, the princess is married off in anger to a man suffering from leprosy; trusting in her husband and in her faith, she remains devoted and confident, and through their shared worship of the Siddhachakra he is healed and the couple prosper.
jainism.explanation: Mayanasundari’s calm certainty that she and her husband will flourish together is a celebrated Jain model of faithful love.
jainism.tie_back: Her confidence echoes the Kural’s ‘we shall live’, though the Jain story credits faith and merit rather than love alone.
jainism.source: Shripal Ras (Vinayavijaya and Yashovijaya, 17th c.), story of Shripal and Mayanasundari (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a popular Jain narrative; a partial match, since the story’s confidence rests on religious faith as much as on mutual love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After twenty years apart, Penelope tests Odysseus with the secret of their marriage bed, carved from a living olive tree; when he describes it, she knows him, and the two are reunited in the home he built.
greek_mythology.explanation: The bed rooted in a living tree is the sign that their love was fixed on both sides throughout the long separation.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope’s long patience could hold because, as the Kural says, the one she loved also loved her.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; mutual love sustaining a separated wife fits, though Homer does not phrase it as a ‘boast’.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that most people, out of ambition, wish to be loved rather than to love, since being loved is close to being honoured, and that people enjoy being loved for its own sake.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle recognises the special satisfaction and standing that comes from being loved.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘pride’ of the loved wife is the same satisfaction Aristotle describes in being loved.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a partial fit, since Aristotle goes on to praise loving over being loved.

kurals.tamil:
வீழப் படுவார் கெழீஇயிலர் தாம்வீழ்வார்
வீழப் படாஅர் எனின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Veezhap paduvaar kezhee-iyilar thaamveezhvaar
veezhap pataa-ar enin.
kurals.meaning: Even a woman admired by everyone is truly unfortunate if the one she loves does not love her back.
kurals.elementary: Imagine everyone at school likes your drawing, but the one person you made it for doesn’t care about it. All the other praise wouldn’t feel like enough. The Kural says love works like that.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a contrast within the same verb: vīḻappaṭuvār, ‘those who are desired’ (by others, or by the world), are kezhīiyilar, ‘not endowed (with good fortune)’, if they are vīḻappaṭār, ‘not desired’, by tām vīḻvār, ‘those whom they themselves desire.’ Parimelazhagar’s line, followed by Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, glosses kezhīiyilar as lacking nalviṉai (the fruit of past merit); Pappaiah sharpens it to being under tīviṉai, while Kalaignar instead reads the lover as lacking the friendly feeling. Pope: ‘Those well-beloved will luckless prove, / Unless beloved by those they love.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, both with the alapeṭai spelling படாஅர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Shakuntala, married in secret to King Dushyanta, comes to his court with her child, but under a curse he fails to recognise her and sends her away; a woman honoured by sages and loved by her forest home is left desolate because the one she loves does not know her.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s heroine is cherished by everyone except the one person whose love she needs.
hinduism.tie_back: Shakuntala’s rejection is the Kural’s point exactly: being loved by many is no fortune without the beloved’s love.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Abhijnanashakuntalam, Act 5 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the play’s famous rejection scene; strong fit, though Dushyanta’s coldness is caused by a curse rather than lack of love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that every gift and achievement counts for nothing without love.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly says every other kind of admiration counts for little without the love that matters most.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV (excerpt); the structure matches, but Paul speaks of having love, not of being loved by a spouse.

islam.quote_or_event: “And you will never be able to be equal [in feeling] between wives, even if you should strive [to do so]. So do not incline completely [toward one] and leave another hanging.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns husbands not to leave a wife ‘hanging’, neither truly married nor free, because his heart has turned away.
islam.tie_back: The neglected wife of this verse, honoured in name but unloved in fact, is the woman the Kural calls unfortunate.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on quran.com (excerpt); good fit on the plight of a wife deprived of her husband’s affection, though framed as a rule for husbands.

judaism.explanation: Michal, a king’s daughter, is one of the few women in the Bible explicitly said to love a man, yet the text never says David loved her in return, and her story ends in estrangement.
judaism.tie_back: A princess with every advantage who is not loved by the man she loves is the Kural’s ‘unfortunate’ in biblical form.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917, excerpt); the one-sidedness is drawn from the wider narrative and the text’s silence, a widely noted reading rather than an explicit statement.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sambula Jataka, Princess Sambula faithfully nurses her husband through a loathsome illness in the forest, but once he is healed and becomes king he neglects her; though she is his chief queen in name, she wastes away until her father intervenes.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka tells of a virtuous queen honoured by all yet left without her husband’s love.
buddhism.tie_back: Sambula is the very woman of this couplet: honoured in every way, yet unfortunate because her husband does not love her.
buddhism.source: Sambula Jataka (Jataka 519) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a canonical Jataka; a strong narrative fit on a revered but unloved wife.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain Ramayana tradition, the princess Anjana is married to Pavananjaya, who, over a misunderstanding, refuses to speak to or look at her for many years; honoured as a queen, she lives in grief until he finally realises his error and returns to her, and she becomes the mother of Hanuman.
jainism.explanation: Anjana’s story is the classic Jain tale of a noble, admired wife who is ignored by the one husband whose love she wants.
jainism.tie_back: Anjana is the Kural’s unfortunate woman exactly: esteemed by all, yet bereft because her beloved does not love her.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 7 (Jain Ramayana), story of Anjana and Pavananjaya (paraphrase; cf. tr. Helen M. Johnson); also in Vimalasuri’s Paumacariya
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative not checked live in this session; strong fit on the admired but unloved wife.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ariadne, the Cretan princess who saved Theseus from the Labyrinth, wakes on the shore of Naxos to find him sailing away, and pours out her grief at being abandoned by the man for whom she gave up everything.
greek_mythology.explanation: A royal heroine with every claim to honour is left wretched because the man she loves has not loved her as she loved him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ariadne illustrates the Kural’s claim that no rank or regard makes up for unreturned love.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a good fit on abandonment, though Ariadne’s story is desertion rather than lifelong indifference.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that the fortunate man still needs friends, since no one would choose to have every good thing on condition of being alone.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, all other goods together cannot make a life happy without the bond of love with others.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural applies the same insight to lovers: all other blessings leave one unfortunate without the beloved’s love.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good structural fit, though Aristotle speaks of friendship in general rather than one beloved.

kurals.tamil:
நாம்காதல் கொண்டார் நமக்கெவன் செய்பவோ
தாம்காதல் கொள்ளாக் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Naamkaadhal kondaar namakkevan seypavo
thaamkaadhal kollaak kadai.
kurals.meaning: If the one I love does not love me in return, what good can he possibly do me?
kurals.elementary: If you keep waving at someone across the playground and they never wave back, the waving can’t make you happy. Love needs someone answering from the other side.
kurals.university: The question form nam(a)kku evaṉ ceypavō, ‘what will they do for us?’, is rhetorical: the heroine admits that her own love (nām kātal koṇṭār, ‘the one we have taken love for’) can bring her nothing if tām kātal koḷḷā kaṭai, ‘when he does not take love (for us).’ Parimelazhagar’s reading, followed by Varadarasanar, makes the implied answer ‘no good at all’; Pappaiah and Kalaignar render ‘what joy will he give?’ The polite plural (koṇṭār, ceypa) keeps the husband at a distance even as she complains. Pope: ‘From him I love to me what gain can be, / Unless, as I love him, he loveth me?’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhramara Gita, a gopi who has been left behind by Krishna sees a bee and addresses it as his messenger, bitterly asking what use his sweet words are when he has forgotten them, and comparing him to a bee that leaves each flower once it has drunk its nectar.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis voice the bitterness of a love that is not answered with presence or care.
hinduism.tie_back: The gopi’s question ‘what good is he to us now?’ is the heroine’s question in the Kural.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; strong fit on the reproach of unreturned love, though theologically Krishna’s love is never truly absent.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that love which only answers love is nothing special, and calls for love that expects no return.
christianity.tie_back: Here Christianity pushes against the Kural’s complaint: the Gospel asks for love that does not depend on being loved back.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; an honest counterpoint rather than a parallel, since Jesus values love without return.

islam.quote_or_event: “O `Abbas ! are you not astonished at the love of Mughith for Barira and the hatred of Barira for Mughith?” … She said, “I am not in need of him.”
islam.explanation: Ibn Abbas recalls Mughith following his freed wife Barira through Medina, weeping, while she refused even the Prophet’s intercession for him.
islam.tie_back: Mughith’s tears show the Kural’s truth: love given to one who does not return it brings nothing but grief.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com (excerpt); near one-to-one on the futility of one-sided love, with the roles of man and woman reversed.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Because the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; for now my husband will love me.”
judaism.explanation: Leah, married to Jacob who loves her sister Rachel, names her firstborn in the hope that this at last will win her husband’s love.
judaism.tie_back: Leah’s repeated longing for a husband who does not love her is the heroine’s question in the Kural lived out across a family history.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917, excerpt); strong fit on love that is not returned within a marriage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sakkapanha Sutta the heavenly musician Pancasikha sings to his lute a love song for Bhadda, who does not return his love, mixing his longing with praise of the Buddha and the arahants; the Buddha remarks on how well the song and the strings agree.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta preserves a song of one-sided longing, set within a discourse that leads toward freedom from desire.
buddhism.tie_back: Pancasikha’s unanswered song is the Kural’s situation: love offered to one who gives nothing back.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a canonical episode; good fit on unrequited love, though the sutta uses it only as a prelude to the Dhamma.

jainism.quote_or_event: Princess Rajimati is betrothed to Arishtanemi, but on the way to the wedding he hears the cries of animals penned for the feast, turns back and renounces the world; Rajimati, grieving, resolves that a love he will not return as a husband can only be followed into renunciation, and becomes a nun.
jainism.explanation: The twenty-second Tirthankara’s story makes the bride’s unreturned love the turning point of her own spiritual life.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati faces the Kural’s question, what can he do for me if he does not love me, and answers it the Jain way, by renunciation.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (Rathanemi) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a canonical Jain narrative not checked live in this session; good fit on love not returned, resolved in a distinctly Jain way.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In her hymn to Aphrodite, Sappho begs the goddess to come again, and recalls Aphrodite smilingly asking whom she must now persuade to love her, promising that one who now flees will soon pursue.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho’s prayer arises because the one she loves does not love her back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine and Sappho share the same ache: love that is not returned brings only pain.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good fit on unrequited love, though Sappho hopes for magic reversal rather than lamenting futility.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that when we love something like ourselves, we strive as far as we can to bring it about that it loves us in return.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, the desire to be loved back is built into the very nature of love.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s question rests on this same law: love naturally seeks its return, and suffers when it fails.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a partial fit, giving the psychological reason behind the Kural’s complaint.

kurals.tamil:
ஒருதலையான் இன்னாது காமம்காப் போல
இருதலை யானும் இனிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Orudhalaiyaan innaadhu kaamamkaap pola
irudhalai yaanum inidhu.
kurals.meaning: Love that sits at one end only is painful; like the load on a carrying pole, it is sweet only when it is balanced at both ends.
kurals.elementary: Have you tried carrying two buckets on a stick across your shoulders? With one bucket it tips and hurts, but with one on each side it’s easy. Love is the same: it feels good only when both people carry it.
kurals.university: This is the Kural’s most famous image for mutual love. Kā is the kāvaṭi or shoulder-pole carried with a load at each end; orutalai (‘one end’) and irutalai (‘two ends’) give Tamil the still-current phrase orutalaik kātal for one-sided love. Kāmam orutalaiyāṉ iṉṉātu, ‘love on one end is painful’, irutalaiyāṉum iṉitu, ‘on both ends it is sweet.’ Parimelazhagar takes the kā simile as governing both halves; Kalaignar spells out that the pole’s two sides must be equally weighted, as love must bloom in both man and woman. Pope: ‘Love on one side is bad; like balanced load / By porter borne, love on both sides is good.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The closing hymn of the Rigveda prays for concord: that those gathered may have a common purpose, hearts in accord and minds alike, so that all may live together in harmony.
hinduism.explanation: The Samjnana hymn makes agreement of hearts the basis of a good shared life.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s balanced carrying pole is the domestic form of this Vedic ideal of hearts in accord.
hinduism.source: Rigveda 10.191.4 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Ralph T.H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; matches the ideal of balanced, shared feeling, though the hymn concerns an assembly, not a couple.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers”
christianity.explanation: Paul uses the image of an unevenly matched yoke to warn against a partnership in which the two sides are not one.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s carrying pole, Paul’s yoke works only when both sides bear equally.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV (excerpt); a striking image parallel, but Paul’s imbalance is of faith, not of love.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi teaches that no lover ever seeks union unless the beloved is also seeking him; the thirst in the lover is matched by a drawing from the other side, as the thirsty seek water and water seeks the thirsty.
islam.explanation: For Rumi true love is never one-sided: longing on one side always implies a pull from the other.
islam.tie_back: Rumi’s mutual seeking is the Kural’s two-ended pole, love sweet because it is carried from both sides.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book III (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Masnavi theme, cited by book only; good fit on mutual love, though Rumi’s beloved is ultimately divine.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him that is alone when he falleth”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth praises the shared load of two who support each other, and pities the one left to carry life alone.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s carrying pole in words: two sides make the burden light, one side makes it painful.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917, excerpt); strong fit on shared burden, though not specific to love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kusa Jataka, the wise but ugly King Kusa loves Princess Pabhavati, who flees from him; he follows her to her father’s city and toils as a potter, basket-maker and cook to be near her, suffering greatly until she finally returns his love.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka dramatises the long misery of a love carried by one side only, and the happiness when it is shared.
buddhism.tie_back: Kusa’s story is the Kural’s carrying pole: unbearable at one end, sweet once both ends bear the weight.
buddhism.source: Kusa Jataka (Jataka 531) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a canonical Jataka; good narrative fit on the pain of one-sided love turning to joy.

jainism.quote_or_event: “But all kinds of objects of the senses, sounds, &c., will cause to the indifferent neither a pleasant nor an unpleasant feeling.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that pain and pleasure come from one’s own attachment, and that the dispassionate are untouched by either.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural seeks balance by making love mutual, Jainism seeks it by laying the burden of attachment down altogether.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; an honest contrast rather than a parallel, since Jainism resolves one-sided love through non-attachment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Themistius tells how Aphrodite’s child Eros would not grow until Themis advised her to give him a brother, Anteros (‘love returned’); with Anteros beside him Eros flourished, but whenever they were parted Eros dwindled again.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes requited love the condition for love to grow at all.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Eros and Anteros are the two ends of the Kural’s pole: love thrives only when it is returned.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a late-antique telling of the myth; strong fit on love needing its counterpart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says goodwill is not yet friendship unless it is returned and each party knows of the other’s goodwill; friendship is goodwill that is reciprocated.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle love on one side only is not yet the real thing; reciprocity is part of its definition.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the philosophical form of the Kural’s claim that love is sweet only when it runs both ways.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known definition; near one-to-one on reciprocity, though Aristotle speaks of friendship rather than romantic love.

kurals.tamil:
பருவரலும் பைதலும் காணான்கொல் காமன்
ஒருவர்கண் நின்றொழுகு வான்.
kurals.transliteration:
Paruvaralum paidhalum kaanaankol kaaman
oruvar-kan nindrozhuku vaan.
kurals.meaning: The god of love works on one side only; does he not see the pain and sorrow he leaves in me?
kurals.elementary: It’s like a game where only one team is allowed to play and the other just has to watch. It doesn’t seem fair. Here the girl feels that love has been fair to her husband but very unfair to her.
kurals.university: Kāmaṉ is the god of love (Sanskrit Kāma, Manmatha), whose flower-arrows awaken desire. The heroine complains that he oruvarkaṇ niṉṟu oḻukuvāṉ, ‘stays and works upon one person only’, i.e. on her, not on her absent husband, and asks whether he does not see her paruvaral (distress) and paital (sorrow). Parimelazhagar’s reading, followed by Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, takes the complaint as against Kāma’s partiality; Pappaiah and Kalaignar connect paital with the pallor (pacalai) of the previous chapter. Pope: ‘While Kaman rushes straight at me alone, / Is all my pain and wasting grief unknown?’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sent by the gods, Kama aims his flower-arrow at the meditating Shiva so that he will love Parvati; Shiva, disturbed, opens his third eye and burns Kama to ashes, leaving Parvati’s love unanswered until she wins him through austerity.
hinduism.explanation: In Kalidasa’s telling, Kama’s arrow stirs longing in one lover while the other remains untouched.
hinduism.tie_back: Parvati, yearning while Shiva is unmoved, is the Kural’s heroine on whom Kama works from one side alone.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known canto; strong fit, the same love-god acting on one side only, though the lovers are divine.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride confesses herself weakened and ill with love.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is likewise laid low by a love that overpowers her body and spirit.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; love-sickness fits, but there is no love-god and the love is not one-sided.

islam.quote_or_event: The women of the city gossip that the governor’s wife has been seeking to seduce her young servant Joseph, saying he has struck her heart with love, while Joseph himself remains unmoved.
islam.explanation: Surah Yusuf portrays a passion that seizes one person entirely while the other stays untouched.
islam.tie_back: As the Kural’s Kama acts on one side only, here love has overpowered one heart and left the other free.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the one-sided seizure of love fits, but the context is illicit desire, not a wife’s longing for her husband.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles, and by the hinds of the field, that ye awaken not, nor stir up love, until it please.”
judaism.explanation: The Song warns that love is a power that should not be roused before its time, because once awakened it cannot be controlled.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has felt love roused in her alone, the danger the Song warns against.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917); love as an independent power fits partly, but there is no one-sidedness or love-god.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Padhana Sutta, Mara approaches the striving Bodhisatta and is answered that Mara’s first army is sensual desire, followed by discontent, hunger and craving; the Bodhisatta resolves not to be overcome by them.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism personifies desire as Mara, also called Kama, whose forces attack the mind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s Kama who torments one person is, in Buddhist terms, Mara’s first army, to be resisted rather than appealed to.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the personified desire matches, but Buddhism treats it as an enemy rather than a god to be reproached.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that suffering comes not from objects or outside powers but from one’s own attachment.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural’s heroine blames Kama for her pain, the Jain text locates its source in her own love itself.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; addresses the same pain but rejects the idea of an external love-god, so only a partial fit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Stung by Apollo’s mockery, Cupid fires two arrows: a golden one that sets Apollo burning with love for the nymph Daphne, and a leaden one that makes Daphne flee from love; Apollo pursues while she escapes, until she is turned into a laurel.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Cupid deliberately makes love one-sided, wounding one heart with desire and the other with aversion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s complaint exactly: the love-god has struck one side only and left the lover to suffer.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; near one-to-one on a love-god making love one-sided.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius describes the lover as wounded by the darts of Venus, so that the wound festers and the craving grows, and he advises against feeding a passion that brings such pain.
philosophy.explanation: Lucretius treats love as a wound inflicted by Venus that torments the one who receives it.
philosophy.tie_back: His wounded lover is the Kural’s heroine struck by Kama, though Lucretius answers with Epicurean detachment.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things 4.1048-1072 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the love-god’s wound matches, but Lucretius’ remedy runs against the Kural’s longing.

kurals.tamil:
வீழ்வாரின் இன்சொல் பெறாஅது உலகத்து
வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Veezhvaarin insol peraaadhu ulakaththu
vaazhvaarin vankanaar il.
kurals.meaning: No one in the world is as hard-hearted, or as brave, as a woman who goes on living without even one kind word from the one she loves.
kurals.elementary: Imagine waiting every day for a letter from someone you love, and none ever comes, yet you keep getting up and going to school. That takes a very strong heart. The Kural says it is almost too strong.
kurals.university: Vaṉkaṇār means both ‘the hard-hearted, cruel’ and ‘the brave, enduring’, and the couplet exploits the ambiguity with self-irony: the heroine says that those who go on living in the world (ulakattu vāḻvār) without receiving (peṟāatu) even a sweet word (iṉcol) from their beloved (vīḻvār) are the most vaṉkaṇ of all. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar read vaṉkaṇmai as the stony endurance of separation; Pappaiah’s ‘no one is more cruel’ and Kalaignar’s ‘no one has so stony a heart’ stress self-reproach, while Pope chooses the heroic sense: ‘Who hear from lover’s lips no pleasant word from day to day, / Yet in the world live out their life,- no braver souls than they!’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Abandoned by her husband Nala in the forest while she sleeps, Damayanti wanders alone through wild country and strange cities for years, without word from him, yet keeps herself alive and devises a way to find him again.
hinduism.explanation: The Nala episode is the great Indian tale of a wife who endures long separation without any message from her husband.
hinduism.tie_back: Damayanti is the Kural’s ‘brave, hard heart’ who goes on living without a single kind word from her beloved.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; good fit on enduring separation without word, though Nala’s desertion is caused by misfortune, not lack of love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs observes how long-delayed hope wears down the heart, while its fulfilment restores life.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine lives in this ‘hope deferred’, waiting for a sweet word that never comes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a good general fit on the strain of waiting, without the specific love context.

islam.quote_or_event: “so patience is most fitting. And Allāh is the one sought for help against that which you describe.”
islam.explanation: Jacob, told that his beloved son Joseph is dead and given no true word of him, chooses beautiful patience.
islam.tie_back: Jacob’s years of patient endurance without news of Joseph parallel the heroine’s enduring life without a word from her beloved.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on quran.com (excerpt); a good fit on enduring separation without word, though the love is a father’s, and Islam praises the patience the Kural half-reproaches.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs teaches that a person’s spirit can sustain him through sickness, but a broken spirit is something no one can bear.
judaism.explanation: The proverb distinguishes bodily suffering, which the spirit can endure, from the wound of the spirit itself.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural marvels that the heroine goes on living with exactly such a broken spirit.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not checked live; a partial fit on the burden of inner suffering, without the love context.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The nun Isidasi recounts how, though she served each husband with complete devotion, she was rejected again and again without cause, until she renounced household life and, as a nun, came to understand the past deeds behind her suffering.
buddhism.explanation: Isidasi’s verses tell of a faithful wife who received no love in return, yet endured and found release.
buddhism.tie_back: Isidasi endured, as the Kural’s heroine does, a life without kind words from those she loved.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a partial fit on enduring unreturned devotion, though Isidasi’s resolution is renunciation.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Jain Ramayana, Sita is sent away into the forest by Rama on account of public rumour, though she is pregnant and innocent; she survives, raises her sons, and when at last recalled to prove her purity she passes the ordeal and chooses to become a nun.
jainism.explanation: The Jain telling shows Sita enduring long abandonment by her husband with dignity and then turning to renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: Sita’s survival without word from Rama mirrors the Kural’s heroine, though the Jain story ends in renunciation rather than longing.
jainism.source: Vimalasuri, Paumacariya (Jain Ramayana), Sita’s banishment and renunciation (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative not checked live in this session; partial fit on enduring abandonment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: For twenty years Penelope receives no word from Odysseus; she weeps nightly for him, weaving and unweaving the shroud to hold off her suitors, and tells the disguised stranger that she wastes her heart away in longing.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope’s endurance without any message from her husband is the Greek model of faithful waiting.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope is the Kural’s ‘brave soul’ who lives on without a single sweet word from her beloved.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong fit on enduring long separation without word, though Penelope is never in doubt of Odysseus’ love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that distance does not dissolve friendship outright but interrupts its activity, and quotes the saying that lack of conversation has broken many a friendship.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, love lives through shared words and company, and withers when communication stops.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine endures exactly what Aristotle says love can hardly survive: no conversation, not even a kind word.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a reasonable fit on the need for words between those who love, though Aristotle speaks of friends in general.

kurals.tamil:
நசைஇயார் நல்கார் எனினும் அவர்மாட்டு
இசையும் இனிய செவிக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Nasai-iyaar nalkaar eninum avarmaattu
isaiyum iniya sevikku.
kurals.meaning: Even if the one I long for shows me no kindness, every word about him, even his very name, is still sweet to my ears.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes when you miss someone, just hearing their name makes you smile, even if they haven’t called you. The girl in this couplet feels that way: anything about him sounds like music.
kurals.university: Nacaiiyār (with alapeṭai) is ‘the one longed for’; nalkār eṉiṉum, ‘even though he grants no grace’; avar māṭṭu icaiyum, ‘even what is heard of / from him’, is iṉiya cevikku, ‘sweet to the ear.’ The word icai is read two ways: as ‘fame, praise’ (Parimelazhagar’s line, followed by Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan and Kalaignar: hearing others praise him is honey to her), or as ‘word, sound’ (Pappaiah: any word from him is sweet). Pope follows the second: ‘Though he my heart desires no grace accords to me, / Yet every accent of his voice is melody.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Venu Gita, the gopis, apart from Krishna as he grazes the cattle in the forest, describe to one another how the sound of his flute enchants them, the deer, the cows and even the rivers.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis find even the distant sound of Krishna’s flute overwhelmingly sweet while they cannot be with him.
hinduism.tie_back: As the heroine finds any word of her beloved sweet, the gopis delight in the far-off music that tells them of Krishna.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good fit on the sweetness of the absent beloved’s sound, though Krishna’s love is not withheld.

christianity.quote_or_event: “let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.”
christianity.explanation: In the Song of Solomon the lover asks only to hear the beloved’s voice, because it is sweet.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that the beloved’s voice and words are sweet to the ear whatever else he gives.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV (excerpt); strong fit on the beloved’s voice as sweetness, though here the love is returned.

islam.quote_or_event: A verse attributed to Majnun says that he passes by the walls of Layla’s dwelling and kisses this wall and that, not for love of the houses, but for love of the one who lives within them.
islam.explanation: Majnun, kept from Layla, finds sweetness in anything connected with her.
islam.tie_back: Majnun’s love for her very walls matches the heroine’s delight in anything heard of her beloved, though he gives her nothing.
islam.source: Attributed to Qays ibn al-Mulawwah (Majnun Layla), Diwan (paraphrase)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely cited verse of uncertain authorship; good fit on cherishing traces of an absent beloved, from Arabic love poetry rather than scripture.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hark! my beloved! behold, he cometh, leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills.”
judaism.explanation: The maiden’s heart leaps at the mere sound of her beloved before she even sees him.
judaism.tie_back: The sound of the beloved delights her just as, in the Kural, every word of him is sweet to the heroine’s ears.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917); strong fit on the sweetness of the beloved’s voice, though he is coming toward her.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Nanda, the Buddha’s half-brother, is led into the order on his wedding day, but he cannot stop thinking of his bride, the Beauty of the Land, who called after him to come back soon; he tells the monks he is discontent because her parting words stay with him.
buddhism.explanation: The Udana tells how a single remembered word from the beloved kept Nanda’s heart bound to her.
buddhism.tie_back: Nanda’s memory of his bride’s words mirrors the heroine’s sense that every word of her beloved is sweet, though the Buddha leads Nanda beyond it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good fit on the lingering sweetness of the beloved’s words, though the roles are reversed and the sutta’s aim is detachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain tradition holds that when a Tirthankara preaches in the samavasarana, his divine sound (divya-dhvani) is understood by every listener in its own language and delights gods, humans and even animals.
jainism.explanation: For Jains the voice of the Jina is the sweetest of all sounds, attracting every being.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine finds her beloved’s words sweet even without his grace; Jainism directs that delight in a voice toward the Jina instead.
jainism.source: Jain doctrine of the samavasarana and divya-dhvani (paraphrase; cf. Tattvartha tradition and the Kalpa Sutra’s account of Mahavira’s preaching)
jainism._accuracy_note: A next-best match only; the shared theme is a beloved voice, but the Jain context is devotional, not romantic, and no specific verse was checked live.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Echo, able only to repeat the last words she hears, falls in love with Narcissus, who rejects her; she follows him, cherishing and repeating his words, and wastes away until only her voice remains.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Echo lives on the words of a beloved who gives her no love in return.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echo is the Kural’s heroine taken to its extreme: his words are all she has, and they are still sweet to her.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; good fit on clinging to the words of an unresponsive beloved.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal writes that the heart has its reasons which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal recognises that love follows its own logic, which argument cannot overturn.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s delight in the words of one who shows her no kindness is just such a reason of the heart.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous maxim; a partial fit on love’s indifference to reasons, though Pascal’s context is faith.

kurals.tamil:
உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய் கடலைச்
செறாஅஅய் வாழிய நெஞ்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Uraaarkku urunoi uraippaai kadalaich
cheraaaai vaazhiya nenju.
kurals.meaning: Bless you, my heart! You keep telling your great pain to one who cares nothing for you; you might as well try to fill up the sea.
kurals.elementary: Imagine trying to fill the ocean with a bucket. No matter how much you pour, it never fills. The girl tells her own heart that telling her sadness to someone who doesn’t care is just like that.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with an apostrophe to the heart (neñcu), a figure that the next chapters develop. Uṟāarkku is ‘to one who is not attached (to you)’, uṟunōy ‘the great affliction (you suffer)’, uraippāy ‘you who tell’; kaṭalaic ceṟāaay is read as an ironic imperative, ‘(go and) fill up the sea!’ Parimelazhagar’s reading, followed by Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan and Kalaignar, is comparative: filling the sea would be easier than winning comfort from the indifferent. Vāḻiya, ‘may you live / bless you’, is half-pitying, half-mocking. Pope: ‘Tell him thy pain that loves not thee? / Farewell, my soul, fill up the sea!’, while his prose gloss reads the sea as her own sea of sorrow. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, both with the triple alapeṭai செறாஅஅய்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A yaksha, exiled from his wife, sees a rain-cloud and pours out his message of longing to it, asking it to carry his words to her; the poet remarks that those tormented by love cannot tell living beings from lifeless things when they make their pleas.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s exile speaks his pain to a cloud that cannot answer, and the poet gently notes the folly of love.
hinduism.tie_back: The yaksha addressing the unhearing cloud is the Kural’s heart telling its pain to one who will not respond.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous opening; strong fit on pouring one’s grief out to something that cannot answer.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride, unable to reach her beloved, begs others to carry word of her lovesickness to him.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she keeps trying to make her pain known to a beloved who has turned away.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the urge to tell one’s love-pain fits, but the Song does not judge it futile.

islam.quote_or_event: The Masnavi opens with the reed flute telling its tale of separation: cut from the reed-bed, it laments, and everyone who hears it weeps, yet few understand its secret.
islam.explanation: Rumi’s reed voices the pain of separation endlessly, to listeners who mostly cannot grasp it.
islam.tie_back: The reed’s endless lament to those who do not understand is the Kural’s heart pouring its sorrow into a sea that never fills.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, opening verses (Song of the Reed) (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; a partial fit, since Rumi’s longing is mystical and his listeners are not indifferent lovers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth uses the sea that never fills as an emblem of endless, unfulfilled effort.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same unfillable sea as the image of telling one’s pain to someone who does not care.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917, excerpt); a close image match on futility, without the love context.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Salla Sutta the Buddha teaches that one does not gain peace of mind by weeping and lamenting; it only brings more pain and wastes the body, and the wise pull out the arrow of grief.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta counsels that pouring out lament does not heal the wound of loss.
buddhism.tie_back: As the Kural tells the heart that pouring out pain to the indifferent is futile, the Buddha says lament itself cannot ease grief.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a good fit on the futility of lament, though the sutta concerns bereavement and offers detachment as the cure.

jainism.quote_or_event: In his dialogue with Indra, the royal sage Nami teaches that if one had countless mountains of gold and silver as big as Mount Kailasa, they would not satisfy a covetous man, for desire is as boundless as space.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana uses the image of endless riches that never satisfy to show that desire cannot be filled.
jainism.tie_back: As the Kural likens telling pain to the indifferent to filling the sea, Nami says desire itself is an emptiness no amount can fill.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 9 (Nami Pravrajya) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase cited by lecture only, not checked live in this session; a partial fit on the unfillable, applied to greed rather than love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Cyclops Polyphemus, in love with the sea-nymph Galatea who will not come to him, sits on the shore singing his pain out over the sea, then rebukes himself, asking where his wits have flown and telling himself to tend his flocks and find another who will love him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Theocritus shows a lover addressing his own heart and recognising the folly of courting one who does not care.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Polyphemus addressing himself by the sea is almost the exact scene of the Kural: a heart told to stop pouring its pain on an indifferent beloved.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known idyll; a strong fit, even sharing the seashore and the self-address.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus teaches that some things are within our power and some are not; other people’s opinions and feelings are not ours to control, and to treat them as if they were brings only frustration and lament.
philosophy.explanation: Stoic wisdom draws the line between what one can change and what belongs to others.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine reaches the Stoic insight that another’s love is not hers to command, and that pleading for it is like filling the sea.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a reasonable fit on the futility of trying to command another’s feelings, though Epictetus is calmer than the Kural’s irony.
